title: How do you make big data feel simple?
subtitle: Redesigning a collaborative analytics platform for data analysts at major banks and insurers

sections.headline: How do you make big data feel simple?
sections.subtext: Datameer's analytics platform was used daily by data analysts at major US, Canadian, and UK banks and insurers. It was powerful and close to impenetrable. My job was to make it usable without dumbing it down.

sections.headline: The starting point
sections.content:
When I joined Datameer in 2016, the platform had been built by engineers, for engineers. The users were data analysts at major banks and insurers — people who understood data deeply, and needed the interface to get out of their way rather than add load on top of already hard analytical work.

The design function existed, but only to execute. Designers received specs and made them look good. There was no research, no design strategy, no seat at the product table. I was hired to change that.

sections.quote: The query builder showed empty results. The full data existed. Users thought the system was broken.
sections.context: The sample-uncertainty problem — the hardest UX challenge on the platform

sections.headline: The core challenge
sections.content:
Big-data analytics has a structural UX problem. When a dataset is too large to process in real time, you work from a sample. But a sample can come back empty — not because the data is missing, but because the sample did not happen to catch it.

Users built a query, saw an empty preview, and assumed their data was gone. They redid work, filed tickets, and lost trust in the tool. The data was fine. The preview was misleading them, not through a bug, but through the nature of sampled data.

This was not a visual problem. It was an information design problem: how do you show uncertainty honestly, without making people stop trusting a tool they depend on every day?

images.alt: The sample-uncertainty feedback design in the query preview
images.caption: The feedback design that tells users a preview is sampled — so an empty result reads as 'sampled', not 'broken'.

steps.label: Customer research
steps.description: I secured exec-sponsored access to visit banks and insurers in the US, joining the sales team on customer site visits. That showed us how analysts actually worked, not how we assumed they did.

steps.label: Platform redesign
steps.description: A full overhaul of the analytics interface, from information architecture to pixel-level craft: column charts, big-data pivot tables, aggregated JSON views, result cards, and a complete filter system.

steps.label: Design system from scratch
steps.description: I built the platform's first design system — a unified visual language for a product that had grown organically for years. Shared components, patterns, and documentation.

steps.label: A seat at the table
steps.description: I moved design from execution-only to a strategic partner, by showing the business value of user research inside a deeply technical product.

sections.headline: What changed

metrics.label: Design's role

metrics.value: Built from scratch — the platform's first

metrics.label: The sampling problem
metrics.value: Honest preview feedback that kept users calibrated instead of alarmed

sections.narrative: The biggest win was not a feature. It was organisational. Design moved from "make it look good" to "help us understand our users." That shift unlocked research access into banks and insurers that had never let a vendor's design team watch their workflows, and those observations went straight into the product roadmap.

sections.headline: What I took from it
sections.content:
The hardest part was not the design. It was earning the credibility to do user research inside banks that treated every outside access as a compliance risk. I had to show that design could think strategically before anyone would let us near a user. The redesign was the proof, and the research access was what it bought.

That is where my conviction comes from: you cannot build a good product without building the organisation that supports it. Teams that actually talk to their users make better products.

executive.summary: Took design from execution-only to a strategic partner at a big-data analytics platform serving major banks and insurers. Built the design system from scratch and solved a fundamental data-uncertainty UX problem.
